idiom_name: generic RenderProp<T> prop or children: (api: Api) => ReactNode
implementation_notes: Mechanically TypeScript is JavaScript - a function-valued prop is called with the state - but the type is the contract: a generic RenderProp<T> alias plus a generic component (<T,>(props: { items: T[]; renderItem: RenderProp<T> })) makes the state arguments inferred at every call site, and the React TypeScript guide's rule that props are described with a type or interface is exactly what turns the deferred-rendering API into self-documentation. Discriminated-union state types keep impossible states out of the render function. Prefer hooks for pure logic reuse exactly as in JavaScript and keep the typed render prop where the owner must own a subtree; in Vue the same typed contract is expressed through typed component declarations and slot props.
pitfalls: A generic component's type parameter must survive the call: annotating the render prop as (item: any) => ReactNode erases inference and defeats the typed alias.
children typed as React.ReactNode does not admit a function; the function-as-children form needs an explicit union or a dedicated prop, otherwise call sites type-error or need casts.
Wrapping a generic component in memo or forwardRef without re-declaring the type parameter silently fixes T to its constraint.

variants.name: Vue scoped slots with a typed state contract
variants.idiom_name: typed state in <script setup lang="ts">, consumed through v-slot slot props
variants.implementation_notes: Vue realizes the pattern through scoped slots, and TypeScript's contribution sits on the child side: the state the child passes to <slot ...> is a typed value from <script setup lang="ts"> - refs, reactive and computed all infer their types, and defineProps/defineEmits declare the component's typed interface - so the slot bindings are the typed contract the parent's v-slot content consumes. The Vue docs describe the scoped slot as a function being passed into the child component and show the equivalent JavaScript call, so the typed slot is the template-side render prop. Keep it for markup that must live in the template and the typed composable when only logic is shared.
pitfalls: Slot props are only as safe as the child's declarations: an undeclared binding the child never passes destructures to undefined, which the template type-checking cannot always catch.
Template slot typing and render-function children do not share one contract; a component mixing both must type each path separately.
Compiled slot functions are recreated per render, so typed inline slot bodies carry the same memoization cost as inline React render props.
